summary: After two iterations, our best approach (greedy init + simulated annealing) scores 88-91 out of 100 on the AHC001 rectangle packing problem. The iter-2 hypothesis that a faster multi-cell initialization would meaningfully improve SA scores was refuted — both init methods produce statistically indistinguishable results (mean 89.9 vs 89.4, within the ~5-point judge variance). SA dominates final quality regardless of starting configuration.
key_points: Best measured scores: 88-91 range across all runs. The SA approach with simple single-edge moves is well-optimized and consistently reaches this band.

Init quality does NOT matter: Multi-cell init (mean 89.9) vs single-cell init (mean 89.4) showed only +0.5 difference, well within the ~5-point run-to-run variance. SA converges to similar quality from either starting point.

Many SA enhancements were tried and failed in iter-2 probes: paired boundary moves (score 0 — buggy), area-biased proposals (85.7), adaptive step sizes (88.2), two-edge moves (89.7), weighted rect selection (85.3). All added overhead that reduced iteration throughput without compensating quality gains.

The scoring function is forgiving — 50% area match gives p=0.75 — so the remaining 9-12 points likely come from rectangles that either miss their target point entirely or have very poor area ratios. Targeted improvements should focus on these worst-case companies.

Next iteration should explore fundamentally different strategies: (1) rectangle swap/exchange moves that let two adjacent companies trade area, (2) a company-priority scheme that gives SA more effort to the worst-scoring rectangles, (3) a completely different representation like power diagrams or weighted Voronoi tessellation converted to axis-aligned rectangles. The current single-edge SA neighborhood may be at its ceiling around 90.
